incidents.title: Eleven nations warn DPRK IT workers use real-time deepfakes in interviews
incidents.outcome: Government alert; no single loss stated.
incidents.confidenceReason: Cited source is TechTimes. The State Department alert (read via the Wayback snapshot 20261110084543; the live page answers 403) says workers use 'the integration of AI, to obfuscate their identities', but on deepfakes only lists as a red flag 'video feeds that appear to be manipulated or artificially generated'. The real-time-deepfake claim in the title is hedged in the primary, and the alert covers a scheme, not one operation.
incidents.summary: The US, Japan, South Korea, France, Germany, Italy and the Netherlands warned that operatives impersonate real people on live video interviews with manipulated feeds.
incidents.quote: North Korean IT Workers Use Real-Time Deepfakes to Beat Hiring Checks, Eleven Nations Warn

harness.note: AI used as an assistant, no agent harness

incidents.title: APT passes an AI agent off as an authorized pentest against a Southeast Asian organization
incidents.actor: Unattributed APT (possibly Earth Lamia, per Trend Micro)
incidents.outcome: Scanning, exploitation, credential harvesting and spraying against the organization.
incidents.confidenceReason: Trend states without hedging that "In one case an AI agent ran its own reconnaissance and lateral movement", in a summary report that shows no evidence. Trend is a security firm, not the model provider, and a firm's one-line statement with no evidence shown is Strong.
incidents.summary: An actor, possibly Earth Lamia, convinced an autonomous AI agent the operation was an authorized penetration test; the agent then ran scanning, exploitation, credential harvesting and password spraying against a Southeast Asian organization.
incidents.quote: In one case tied to a possible Earth Lamia operation, they jailbroke an autonomous AI agent that then conducted its own network scanning, exploitation, credential harvesting, and password spraying against a target in Southeast Asia.
incidents.singleSourceReason: Only Trend Micro has reported this operation among the sources found in the 2026-11-17 sweep.

incidents.title: CyberXero initial access broker runs 51 Claude Code agents plus PentAGI
incidents.targets: Ukrainian energy and utilities, plus mass WordPress/e-commerce scanning
models: PentAGI via an AI provider API
incidents.outcome: Data on 628,000+ Ukrainian individuals held; four organizations had confirmed exfiltration; no confirmed sale of access.
incidents.confidenceReason: SOCRadar analyzed an exposed open directory with agent configs and session logs documenting the AI use.
incidents.summary: The actor's workstation ran a swarm of 51 specialised Claude Code agents, and the team server wired PentAGI to Cobalt Strike. Logs record a fictional 'authorized pentest' narrative built to avoid model refusals; the Ukrainian campaign itself was largely manual.
incidents.quote: An AI orchestration layer: up to 51 specialized Claude Code agents on the primary workstation, plus a PentAGI deployment wired into a Cobalt Strike Team Server through an AI provider API
incidents.singleSourceReason: Only SOCRadar has reported this operation among the sources found in the 2026-11-17 sweep.

incidents.title: Open-source Hermes and OpenClaw agents used against the Taiwanese government
incidents.actor: Suspected China-linked hackers (Taiwan did not attribute)
incidents.targets: Taiwanese government agencies (85 credentials, 2,564 personnel records)
incidents.outcome: Taiwanese government agencies were attacked from 1 to 4 July 2026.
incidents.confidenceReason: Dream "uncovered the complete operational workspace" (1,395 files) of a Hermes and OpenClaw framework that "achieved confirmed, real-world compromises against state infrastructure" on 1-4 July 2026. That is direct observation. CyberScoop quotes Dream's post verbatim ("The attacker didn't stop at primary targets ...") and credits the Financial Times with naming Taiwan as the target. Dream itself names no country: the grade rests on Dream's evidence, and the Taiwan link on the Financial Times.
incidents.summary: Attackers used the open-source Hermes and OpenClaw agent frameworks against government agencies, and Dream recovered the framework's operational workspace. The Taiwan attribution comes from the Financial Times via CyberScoop; Dream's own report names no country. Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs described a hybrid of manual and AI agent-assisted attacks.
incidents.quote: The hackers used two popular open-source AI frameworks, Hermes and OpenClaw, to set up the Taiwan operation.

sources.title: Suspected Chinese hackers use open-source Hermes and OpenClaw agents against the Taiwanese government

incidents.title: Hermes AI agent automates post-exploitation inside Thailand's Ministry of Finance
incidents.outcome: Post-exploitation inside the ministry; the ministry had not publicly confirmed a breach.
incidents.confidenceReason: Hunt.io found the agent's logs in the operator's exposed directories: "The Hermes logs found within the three directories capture the agent enumerating ministry hosts", and "Hermes output logs show the operator ran the agent in unattended or YOLO mode". That is direct observation. The ministry has not confirmed a breach, which bears on the outcome, not on the AI use.
incidents.summary: Recovered logs showed attackers used the Hermes agent, in unattended mode per Hunt.io, to automate parts of an intrusion at Thailand's Ministry of Finance.
incidents.quote: Five recovered Hermes call logs show the agent was used to find a way to elevate privileges, scan for kernel vulnerabilities, enumerate services, search for SUID and SGID binaries, inspect containers, and traverse file systems.

incidents.title: TuxBot v3: Keksec-linked IoT botnet built with LLM help
incidents.outcome: A working IoT botnet framework with Telnet brute force and DDoS.
incidents.confidenceReason: Unit 42 infers LLM authorship from an unremoved LLM safety disclaimer and chain-of-thought comments in the code.
incidents.summary: Unit 42 recovered the TuxBot v3 framework, whose 61 C files carry an unremoved LLM safety disclaimer and chain-of-thought comments; about 70 percent works.
incidents.quote: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 identified a previously undocumented modular IoT botnet framework called TuxBot v3 Evolution, and it comes with an unusual detail: the developer used a large language model to write significant portions of the code, and the LLM’s safety disclaimer ended up in every compiled binary.
